script: The school janitor came to my graduation and sat in the back row where nobody would see him. I did not invite him. My parents were not there either. My mother left when I was nine, and my father worked nights forty minutes away, so from about eleven I got myself to school and I got myself home. Mr. Alvarez opened the building at five in the morning. By the time I was twelve I was there at five thirty, waiting by the gym doors, because our apartment had no heat that winter and the school did. He never asked why. He just started unlocking the side door instead of the front one, so I would not have to walk around the building in the cold. Then there was the food. One morning he handed me a paper bag and said the cafeteria had over ordered. He said that every single morning for four years. A cafeteria does not over order for one thousand four hundred days. When I was sixteen I told him I was dropping out. He did not argue. He asked one question. He asked what my father wanted. Two weeks later a scholarship application appeared in my locker with the deadline circled in pen. I never asked who put it there. I got it. Four years later I stood in a gown in that same gymnasium and looked at the back row, and there he was, in his work shirt, straight from a shift. He did not clap. He sat with his hands folded and looked at the floor, the way a man does when he thinks the moment is not his. Afterward I found him already picking up dropped programs. Still working. I said his name. He said congratulations, and that he should let me get back to my family. I told him my family was standing right there. He said he was just the guy who opened the doors. So I told him what I worked out in college. That a cafeteria does not over order for four years. That I counted. One thousand four hundred and twelve mornings. He looked at the programs in his hand like he had forgotten them. Then he set them down on a chair, unfinished, which I had never once seen him do.
